{"number":1264,"title":"Delete the two-name settings-file tolerance once no member carries .claudinite-checks.json","body":"Phase 3 of #1252. The rename landed with every reader in the corpus accepting **both** settings-file names, because a member renames its own file only on the converge that carries `engine/migrations/2026-08-23-settings-file-rename`. This issue is the removal of that tolerance.

## The precondition — a converge-cycle fact, never a date

Do not open this on a calendar. The condition is: **no member still carries `.claudinite-checks.json`**, confirmed by reading the fleet's own artifacts rather than assumed from elapsed time. Retiring a tolerance while a member is still on the old shape does not just leave that member behind — every reader then finds no settings file at all, which reads as "declares no packs, never adopted", silently, with green runs to show for it (the same class as #1106).

The sheepdog roster walk already reads each member's declaration under both names, so the cheapest confirmation is to have it report which name each member answered on.

## What comes out

- `engine/settings-file.mjs`: `LEGACY_SETTINGS_FILE`, and `SETTINGS_FILES` collapses to the one name. Everything downstream that maps over it becomes a single path.
- `engine/checks/helpers/repo-context.mjs`: `LEGACY_CONFIG_KEYS` (`claudinite`, `maintenance`) and the two fold-in branches that read them — the legacy `packVersions` map, `claudinite.engineVersion`, and `maintenance.delivery` → `dailyClaudiniteUpdatesRequirePrReview`. A member still declaring either then gets the unknown-setting error, which is correct once none does.
- `engine/installed-versions.mjs`: `LEGACY_STAMP_KEY` and its read path.
- `engine/checks/helpers/repo-context.mjs`: `LEGACY_ENDPOINTS_KEY`, and `SCHEDULE_KEYS` drops `endpoints`.
- `engine/scheduler/land-pr.mjs`: `resolveDelivery`, `deliveryFromChecks`, and `deliveryFor`'s `maintenance.delivery` fallback — gated separately on no fielded vendored worker still importing them (walk the trunk's pack history, per the `updates/*` rule).
- `engine/served-by.mjs`: same gate, same walk. Nothing in canon calls it now.
- The both-name reads in `fleet-api.mjs`, `fleet-reads.mjs`, `signals/fleet.mjs`, `packs/claudinite-dashboard/settings-read.mjs`, `seeds-agree.mjs`, `adopt-pack/checks.mjs`, `selftest.mjs`, and the older migration records that read the declaration.
- The `legacy-settings-name` rehearsal fixture, and the assertion in `rehearsal.test.mjs` that requires exactly one fixture to carry the retired name.
- The retired name in the two `except` lists (`packs/claudinite-lifecycle/declared-checks.json`, `packs/product-wiki/declared-checks.json`), the dashboard stub's `paths:`/`hashFiles`, and the `find` in `environment-setup-command.sh`.

The last three are the ones to check by hand rather than by grep: a stub is copied into a member once and never re-copied, and the setup script is pasted into a container by hand, so both outlive a member's converge by an unknown margin. They come out last, or not at all.

{"number":1260,"title":"Verify in production: a real member converges onto engine 60822.1 and then the convention-shaped packs","body":"#1246 landed on #1248. A pack manifest now takes `id`, `prose`, `badge`, `skills`, `worldRules` and `workRules` from its own directory, and a pack that declares no `detect`/`marker` carries no fingerprint. Coded rules moved into `/worldRules/` and `/workRules/`; a pack's tests moved into `/test/`, which the vendor set now drops by name.

**Why this could not be watched now.** The delivery ORDER is the thing at risk, and it only exists on a real member. A manifest with no `id` is dropped outright by a pre-convention loader — which fails that member's mount self-test and stops it converging at all, the #1004 failure shape. The guard is `minEngineVersion`: every pack version rose to `60822.1`, and the pack update flow treats a violation as a terminal rather than a "try anyway". So a member must land engine `60822.1` FIRST, and only then receive the packs.

The canary rehearsal ([run 32608725317](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/actions/runs/32608725317)) proved the happy end state — a canon whose packs declare no `id` converges and passes a member's self-test. It proves nothing about the ordering, because the rehearsal restores the tree and never stamps: no member's `packVersions` or `engineVersion` has actually moved. That is what this verifies, on the first nightly converge that reaches one.

Original-issue: #1246
In-production-when: `missingbulb/ClaudiniteCanary`'s `.claudinite/claudinite.json` stamps `engineVersion` at `60822.1` or above.
Verify: on that same member and at that same commit, read its stamped `packVersions` and its mount. Pass requires all three: (a) `packVersions.basics` is `60822.1` or above — the packs followed the engine rather than being held back or, worse, landing ahead of it; (b) `.claudinite/shared/packs/basics/worldRules/` exists in the mount and `.claudinite/shared/packs/basics/file-placement.mjs` does not — the pack tree that arrived is the convention-shaped one; (c) `.claudinite/shared/packs/basics/test/` does not exist — the vendor set dropped the test directory by name. Any of the three failing is a fail: report which, with the paths and versions actually read.
Not-before: 2026-08-24T06:00:00Z
Retry-every: 1 day

Model: sonnet

---

- **Live** → run `Verify:`. Passes: comment the versions and paths actually read, and close this issue as completed. Fails: reopen #1246 with a comment saying what was asserted, what was found instead, and where you read it; comment here linking that; close this issue as completed — finding the fault is this verification working.
- **Not yet live** → push `Not-before:` forward by `Retry-every:`, clear this issue's `task:status:*` label, and leave it open. No comment; the bumped field is the record.

{"number":1256,"title":"wiki-growth: drop the product-wiki-growth label, gate on open PRs' changed paths","body":"The `product-wiki-growth` label exists for exactly one reason: the wiki-growth precondition declines while a previous round's PR sits unreviewed, and the label is how it recognises that PR. It buys nothing else, and every growth PR carries a marker whose only reader is the next week's precondition.

The same gate reads off content instead: decline while any open PR has a pending change under `product-wiki/`. Structural, no marker to apply, and it also catches a human's own wiki edit in flight — which the label never could.

Work:
- `prs` signal collector resolves each open PR's changed paths.
- wiki-growth precondition declines on a `product-wiki/` path in any open PR; `GROWTH_LABEL` and the labels field it was the only reader of go away.
- `task.md`: stop instructing the worker to label the PR.

{"number":1253,"title":"Verify in production: the dashboard's lead block and its day picker","body":"#1251 landed a lead region on both dashboard pages: a **Start here** card naming the one piece of work most worth doing, priced by what its park asks of a person, and — on the fleet page — the morning brief with a `‹ ›` picker back through earlier days.

The ranking, the pricing and the card's own rendering are covered by unit tests that ran. What is **not** provable here is the half that only exists in a browser against real data: the page wiring (`view-fleet.mjs`'s `renderBrief`/`readDay` and the picker's buttons, `view-repo.mjs`'s lead), which no test exercises, and which this repo cannot watch because the dashboard is a static page that reads GitHub live as its signed-in viewer, deployed from whichever repo declares the `claudinite-dashboard` pack — not from here.

Original-issue: #1249

Verify: on the deployed site, `index.html` contains `id="fleet-lead"`, `id="lead-digest-section"` and `id="digest-nav"`, and `next-work.mjs` and `ui.mjs` are served (200) — that much is an automatic read and must pass on its own. Then, because the page renders nothing without a signed-in viewer and no unattended read can reach that state, one person's step, spelled out: open the fleet dashboard signed in, and confirm (a) the **Start here** card at the very top names a repo and an issue with a minutes figure beside the reason — or reads "Nothing is waiting on you" if the fleet is clean — and (b) clicking `‹` in the morning brief loads the day before and `›` returns to yesterday. A pass is both halves; a fault in either is a fail.

{"number":1225,"title":"The hourly scheduler cron is the fleet's whole Actions allowance — move to a twice-daily tick","body":"## The problem

The August usage report puts `claudinite-scheduler.yml` at 1,515 of 2,123 private Actions minutes — **71% of spend** — running at a near-identical ~26 min/day on every private member (MissingBulbWebsite 26.1, WIP 27.0, hitbut 26.0, ClaudiniteWebsite 25.2, EdFringeAllocator 17.0).

Four private members × 24 min/day × 30d = 2,880 min = **$17.28/mo**, which is exactly the $18.00 allowance the report terminates at. The scheduler *is* the allowance, with zero macOS and zero real work. It scales linearly with adoption: WIP and hitbut came online Aug 20–21 and immediately added ~53 min/day between them.

## Why optimising the job buys nothing

Sampled 30 consecutive scheduled runs on this repo: **median 32s wall-clock**, only one over 60s. Actions bills each job rounded up to the whole minute, so ~46% of every billed minute is already rounding waste.

The cost is **run count**, not compute. The only lever is fewer runs.

## What the 24 runs/day are actually buying

Exactly one task in the corpus is `hourly` — `usage-fold` (`packs/claudinite-growth`). Everything else is `daily-2h`/`daily-1h`/`daily`/`daily+1h`/`weekly`/`monthly`/`manual`. Per `engine/scheduler/calendar.mjs`, the whole daily family lands at `dailyHour-2 … dailyHour+1`, with weekly and monthly also at `dailyHour` — so a default member's entire anchor set is four clock hours a day.

Two of the three remaining jobs are already solved elsewhere in the engine:

- **Ordering within a repo.** `after:` shipped (`engine/scheduler/task-contract.mjs:184-192`); `growth-extract` declares it and its own comment says the staggered hours *"express the same intent and cannot enforce it; this can."*
- **Chain continuation.** `executor.mjs:215` re-reads the queue each iteration and calls `readyDependents()` on every close, so a multi-stage chain drains back-to-back in one run.

That leaves adopting newly-marked ad-hoc issues, `Not-before` releases, and dead-claim reclaims as the only work the 23 extra runs a day exist for.

## The end state

`docs/tasks-dispatch/DESIGN.md` §17, with the measured trade and the rejected alternatives. Cron fires twice daily at ` ,<(dailyHour+12)%24>`. **24 runs/day → 2**; $17.28/mo → $1.44/mo; a new private member costs 2 min/day instead of 26.

---

# The plan

## Phase 0 — out-of-band setup: **none**

Verified there is no human-only step. No new secret, permission, repo variable or platform setting. The one path a converge cannot push into is `.github/workflows/`, and that is already solved: `pendingSchedulerWorkflow` (`updates/pack-update.mjs:161`) computes the target and **withholds** it, and the `update` task's apply stage lands it through the member's own PR lane. The cron rewrite reaches every member on the existing nightly cycle with nobody in the loop.

## Phase 1 — the approved stack (one review pass)

All code written before approval is asked for, including the destructive tail.

- [ ] **PR A — #1226 (open).** Design + simulator: `cronHours`, S67–S73, DESIGN §17, coverage rows. Closes #1227.
      *Exit:* merged.
- [ ] **PR B — the vocabulary.** Split `FREQUENCIES` (what a NEW declaration may name) from an accept-at-the-door set, with **one normalization door at declaration load** — not inside `anchorInstant`, because `periodMs` also feeds the janitor's stale-ready bound (`queue/janitor-rules.mjs:103`) and the signal window (`queue/signals.mjs:15`); normalizing only the anchor judges a daily task stale after two hours. Four consumers: `calendar.mjs:25`, `task-contract.mjs:100`, `packs/claudinite-growth/task-declaration-shape.mjs:49` (rejects the retired tokens for new declarations), `slots.mjs:23` (fielded shim, stays).
      Four declarations move: `update` `daily-2h`→`daily`; `growth-extract` `daily-1h`→`daily` (already has `after:`); `fleet-digest` `daily+1h`→`daily` + a new `after:` naming the sheepdog sweeps (safe cross-pack — an undeclared upstream yields no constraint); `usage-fold` `hourly`→`daily` **and its `WINDOW_DAYS = 2/24` must move with it**, or the "session captured" half of its precondition goes permanently dark and a repo whose only movement is commit-less sessions never folds again.
      Plus the cross-repo stagger `after:` cannot express: **set this repo's `taskScheduler.dailyHour` to 5**, so members extract at 04:00 and the canon's `growth-promote` reads their merged mains at 05:00. One line, this repo only, no fleet migration. Add `after: ['claudinite-growth/growth-extract']` to the canon-local `growth-promote` for the within-repo half.
      *Exit:* merged, suite green, S74 (normalized `hourly` behaves as `daily`) added and passing.
- [ ] **PR C — the cron.** `hashedCron` returns two hours derived from `dailyHour`; `converge-wiring.mjs:132` passes the schedule; the vendored stub's placeholder and **the canon's own `.github/workflows/claudinite-scheduler.yml` change in the same commit** — the canon has no converge, so its copy drifts invisibly otherwise.
      *Exit:* merged; this repo's own workflow reads the two-hour cron.
- [ ] **PR D — the destructive tail, written now, merged later.** Retire the door-normalization and drop the legacy tokens from the accepted set. Body states its merge is gated on Link 3 and names it.
      *Exit:* approved in this pass; **not merged**.

## Phase 2 — the execution chain

Filed as sub-issues of this tracker once the plan is agreed, each naming the previous in `Blocked-by:` so the queue does the waiting.

- [ ] **Link 1 — force delivery and read it back.** Drive Shepherd's `fleet-baseline` with `follow`.
      *Ready when:* PRs B and C are merged.
      *Worked when:* every member's stamp shows the new `packVersions`, **and** its `.github/workflows/claudinite-scheduler.yml` cron reads ` H,H+12` for that member's own `dailyHour`. Read per member; a member that cannot be read parks the link open rather than passing — a scope-blocked sweep answers "all clear" exactly like a healthy one.
- [ ] **Link 2 — verify in production.** *Ready when:* Link 1 closed and one full UTC day has passed.
      *Worked when:* each private member's Actions usage shows exactly **2** scheduler runs for that day (baseline: 24), and no task's standing item is missing its occurrence. Also the first read of the risk the sim cannot model — whether a member's whole daily chain now fits one drain against `timeout-minutes: 350`.
- [ ] **Link 3 — retire the tolerance.** *Ready when:* Link 2 closed **and** no member's task declarations still name a retired token — a converge-confirmable precondition, never a calendar date: retiring it while a member still declares `hourly` turns that member's daily task into a two-hour staleness park.
      *Worked when:* PR D merged, suite green.

## Known residual risks

- **Dropped ticks cost 12× more latency** (S71). Nothing is stranded — dueness comes from the anchor, never from whether the cron fired — but a dropped anchor tick now waits until the drain tick. This is why the second tick is not optional.
- **Ad-hoc latency goes to a 6h mean / 12h worst case** (S68). An `issues: [labeled]` trigger would take it to seconds for a run only when a mark happens; recorded in §17.5 as additive and deliberately out of this plan's scope.
- **A whole day now settles serially in one Actions job.** The simulator's durations are fixtures, so it cannot say whether a real member's chain fits. Link 2 is the first real measurement.

{"number":1237,"title":"Chain 3/3: retire the twice-daily-cron migration tolerances","body":"Link 3 of #1225's execution chain — the last one, and the **delayed task that merges #1234**. Everything you need is here.

```
Blocked-by: #1236
Retry-every: 7 days
Model: sonnet
```

## What this removes

#1234 is written, reviewed, rebased onto `main` and mergeable. It empties `LEGACY_FREQUENCIES`, so `hourly` / `daily-2h` / `daily-1h` / `daily+1h` stop being accepted in a task declaration, and it stops `scheduler-workflow-shape` accepting the legacy hourly cron.

**It must not be merged early, and the reason is measurable.** `scheduler-workflow-shape` is severity `blocking`; on #1234's branch it emits a finding for an hourly cron; and a member's converge **withholds** `.github/workflows/` — the one path it cannot push — so a member holding the old cron cannot fix itself. Merging before every member's workflow PR has landed turns the whole fleet red on a file none of them can repair.

## What makes this step's world ready

#1236 closed, **and** the precondition below reads true. Converge-confirmable, never a date — if it does not hold yet, this is a wait, not a failure.

**No member's own task declarations still name a retired frequency.** Canon packs are already migrated; what matters is each member's `.claudinite/local/packs/*/tasks/*/task.mjs`, which is member-authored and which no vendoring pass rewrites. Grep each member for `frequency: 'hourly'`, `'daily-2h'`, `'daily-1h'`, `'daily+1h'`.

Retiring early does not merely fail such a task. `periodMs` also feeds the janitor's stale-ready bound and the precondition's signal window, so an un-normalized token makes a daily task judged against a bound it was never sized for — a `needs-human` park on every sweep.

## The playbook

1. Check the precondition across every member. If any still declares a retired token: comment which member and which file on #1225, push `Not-before` forward by `Retry-every`, clear this issue's `task:status:*` label, and leave it open. No other comment — the bumped field is the record. Fixing that member's declaration is the way to unblock this, and is worth doing.
2. Precondition holds → fetch #1234's branch and confirm it is still current against `main`; rebase if `main` has moved under it.
3. Run the full suite: `node --test $(git ls-files '*.test.mjs')`, and `check_the_work`.
4. Green → merge #1234 (squash).

**Already done, 2026-08-22 — do not redo:** the branch was rebased onto `main` after #1230 merged, and the `pack-version-bumped` false green called out in #1234's body is resolved — `claudinite-lifecycle` is `60822.3` against main's `60822.2`, and `check_the_work` is clean against the true base. Step 2 is a re-check, not the original rebase.

Note the two tolerances have **different** gates. The cron half's gate — every member's workflow PR landed — is satisfied by #1235. If the frequency half is still blocked long after, split the commit and merge the cron half alone.

## What counts as this step having worked

#1234 merged, suite green, and no member red on its next converge.

## How it ends

Comment on #1225 that the tolerances are retired and the migration is complete, then close this issue as completed. #1225 can close with it.

{"number":1240,"title":"Remove the tidy-branches task from tidy-repo","body":"Drop `tidy-branches` from the `tidy-repo` pack. The pack keeps its other two dimensions, `tidy-issues` and `tidy-prs`; only the branch sweep goes.

## The change

Delete `packs/tidy-repo/tasks/tidy-branches/` (both `task.mjs` and `task.md`) and sweep every reference to it. Known referencing files:

- `packs/tidy-repo/pack.mjs` — the task roster
- `packs/tidy-repo/pack.test.mjs` — assertions naming the task
- `packs/tidy-repo/README.md`
- `packs/tidy-repo/RULES.md` — names the three tasks and the "branches — assess only" half of the policy
- `packs/tidy-repo/tasks/tidy-issues/task.md` — mentions it
- `packs/tidy-repo/skills/single-branch-status/SKILL.md` — its worker skill

{"number":1236,"title":"Chain 2/3: verify the twice-daily cron in production — 2 scheduler runs a day, not 24","body":"Link 2 of #1225's execution chain. Everything you need is here.

```
Blocked-by: #1235
Not-before: 2026-08-25T06:00:00Z
Retry-every: 1 day
Model: sonnet
```

## What this proves

The whole point of the change: the scheduler was **71% of private Actions spend** at ~26 min/day per member, because Actions bills each job rounded up and the cron fired 24 times a day to do about 13 minutes of work. Two ticks a day should make that ~2 min/day. Nothing so far has measured a real repo — only the simulator.

## What makes this step's world ready

#1235 closed (every member on the new cron), **and** at least one full UTC day has elapsed since, so there is a complete day to count.

## What to observe

For each **private** member — the ones that cost anything; public repos are free and unlimited:

1. **The count.** Scheduler workflow runs for one complete UTC day. Expect exactly **2**. Baseline: 24.
2. **Nothing was dropped.** No task's standing item is missing its occurrence for that day — a cheaper cron that quietly stopped instantiating work is a regression, not a saving.
3. **The risk the simulator could not model.** A whole day's chain now settles serially inside one executor run. Read the longest executor run's duration against the workflow's `timeout-minutes: 350`. The simulator's task durations are fixtures, so this is the first real read of whether a member's day actually fits.

## What counts as this step having worked

Every private member shows 2 scheduler runs for the measured day, no missing occurrences, and no executor run near its timeout.

## When the check fails

Comment what you read and **leave this issue open** — closing releases the next link.

- Still 24 runs on some member → its workflow never landed; reopen #1235's question there rather than proceeding.
- Missing occurrences → this is a real regression in the cadence change. Reopen #1225 with what is missing and stop the chain.
- An executor run near the timeout → do **not** fail the step, but say so plainly on #1225: it is the residual risk the plan named, and it wants its own issue rather than silence.

## How it ends

Comment the per-member figures on #1225 — runs/day before and after, and the longest executor run — then close this issue as completed. That close releases Link 3.

{"number":1235,"title":"Chain 1/3: force the twice-daily cron onto every member, and read it back","body":"Link 1 of #1225's execution chain. You will never see the conversation that planned this — everything you need is here.

```
Blocked-by: #1231
Model: sonnet
```

## What changed, and why this needs forcing

The scheduler cron went from hourly to twice daily (`docs/tasks-dispatch/DESIGN.md` §17): ` ,<(dailyHour+12)%24> * * *`. That is a change to a contract members' own files must satisfy — a workflow file plus a frequency vocabulary — so the nightly converge is not enough on its own to answer *"did it work on every repo?"*.

## What makes this step's world ready

#1231 closed, meaning #1230 merged. The queue holds this until then.

## The playbook

1. Drive Shepherd's `fleet-baseline` with `follow`, so it converges every member and reports per member rather than dispatching and returning.
2. For **each** member, read two things from the member's own repo:
   - its stamp's `packVersions` — `claudinite-lifecycle` ≥ `60822.2`, `claudinite-growth` ≥ `60822.1`, `claudinite-dashboard` ≥ `60822.2`;
   - its `.github/workflows/claudinite-scheduler.yml` `cron:` line.
3. The cron is member-specific. Compute the expected value rather than matching a constant: `node engine/scheduler/hash-minute.mjs ` for the minute, and the member's own `taskScheduler.dailyHour` (default 4) for the hours — so a default member expects ` 4,16 * * *`.

## What counts as this step having worked

Every member reads back **both** the stamped pack versions and its own correct two-tick cron.

The workflow file is the half that can lag: `.github/workflows/` is the one path a converge cannot push, so it lands through the member's `update` task apply-stage PR. A member whose stamp has moved but whose workflow PR is still open has **not** passed — note it and keep this issue open; it will pass on a later run once that PR lands.

## When the check fails

Comment what you actually read, per member, and **leave this issue open**. Closing is what releases the next link, so a failed step must not close.

A member you cannot read is a failure, not a pass. A scope-blocked or rate-limited sweep answers "all clear" in exactly the way a healthy fleet does — if a read did not succeed, say so rather than counting it.

## How it ends

Comment the per-member evidence on #1225, then close this issue as completed. That close releases Link 2.

{"number":1224,"title":"Eliminate avoidable GitHub-platform assumptions from packs","body":"A census of GitHub-platform assumptions (the platform, not plain git) across the engine and every pack found 367 distinct assumptions counted once per component — 81 in the engine, 286 across the packs.

Scoping this work to the packs, and excluding `git-github` (which owns GitHub as a subject, 38 assumptions), leaves ~248 in scope. Of those, roughly 40–50 are avoidable and fall in two buckets:

**Bucket 1 — not actually GitHub assumptions (~13).** Generic-CI facts phrased in GitHub vocabulary, which the census counts only because the wording names a GitHub feature. They hold on any CI system:

- `firebase` (4) — "release-workflow variables", "workflow dispatch"
- `web-scraping` (3) — runner IP blocks, "repository secrets", commit-step durability
- `macos` (2) — secret-gated signing lane, build annotations
- `spec-driven-product` (2) — CI-gated merge, automated release cut
- `aws-sam` (1) — deploy-workflow staleness caveat
- `research-project` (1) — branch/commit/PR conventions

The fix is a phrasing pass to platform-neutral wording. No behavior changes.

**Bucket 2 — restatements of facts another pack or skill owns (~25–30).** These violate the corpus's own dependency rule ("say what A needs from B; don't re-spell how B does its job"). Repeat offenders:

- "`GITHUB_TOKEN` cannot write `.github/workflows/`" — re-explained in `claudinite-dashboard`, `claudinite-fleet-sheepdog`, `claudinite-lifecycle` when the engine's withhold lane owns it
- "`GITHUB_TOKEN` pushes fire no workflows" — re-derived in `claudinite-dashboard`, `chrome-extension`, `static-website` when `git-github` owns it
- the exact-title-tracker / issue-creation-lands-open / no-comment-update-tool cluster — owned by the `unattended-agents` skill, restated in `tidy-repo`, `jwt`, `product-wiki`
- squash-merge evidence rules — owned by `git-github`, restated in `basics` and `tidy-repo` skills

Two exemptions constrain this bucket: vendored workflow stubs must stay self-contained (their comments travel into member repos, where a canon reference dangles), and `task.md` files are read standalone by executor sessions, so some restatement there is deliberate context rather than drift.

**Out of scope.** The remaining ~200 are inherent — the dashboard's rate-limit/OAuth/Pages model, sheepdog's fleet API vocabulary, lifecycle's PR delivery, growth's issue-queue semantics, the two vendored release pipelines, basics' issue→PR lifecycle, tidy-repo's triage primitives. Eliminating those means dropping the capability or building a forge-abstraction seam, neither of which is justified without a second consumer. The per-pack REST-client duplication is likewise deliberate (#959).

**Done when** both buckets are landed and a re-run of the per-component census shows the reduction.","state":"open","html_url":"https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/issues/1224","user":{"login":"missingbulb","id":73882448,"profile_url":"https://github.com/missingbulb","avatar_url":"https://avatars.githubusercontent.com/u/73882448?v=4"},"author_association":"OWNER","assignees":[],"comments":1,"reactions":{"total_count":0,"+1":0,"-1":0,"laugh":0,"confused":0,"heart":0,"hooray":0,"rocket":0,"eyes":0},"created_at":"2026-08-22T11:21:03Z","updated_at":"2026-08-22T11:24:29Z","has_parent":false,"has_children":false,"closed_by_pull_requests":{"total_count":0,"references":[]}}

```
Original-issue: #1214

The between-items read only happens after a settle, so a run that found nothing pickable proves nothing and does not satisfy this.
Verify: read that run's log. (2) Count `Claudinite executor` workflow runs in the 24h after the merge and in the 24h before it. Assert the after-count is lower. If it is not, say so with both counts and reopen Original-issue — the change's whole premise is that it is.
Not-before: 2026-08-23T12:00:00Z
Retry-every: 1 day
Model: sonnet
```

{"number":276,"title":"Move chrome-extension-release plumbing out of core `.github/` into the pack (vendored into consumers)","body":"Resolves the **RELEASE** item of #270: the reusable release workflows (`.github/workflows/chrome-extension-*.yml` + `deploy-privacy-page.yml`) and the three composite actions (`read-release-config`, `bump-extension-patch`, `report-failure`) live in Claudinite's core tree but exist solely for the `chrome-extension-release` pack. They must move behind the pack that owns them, leaving Claudinite with no release-specific GitHub Actions.

## Decision (agreed with owner)

- **Hosting model: vendor into each consumer.** GitHub only resolves reusable workflows/composite actions from a repo's own `.github/`, never from a `packs/…` subdir, so "into the pack" means the pack holds the templates and each consumer hosts a *managed* copy in its own `.github/`. Consumers become self-contained; baselining (not the consumer) owns keeping the copies correct. This reverses the original "thin consumer" design — deliberately.
- **Phase-2 deletion: automatic, telemetry-gated.** Once the fleet census confirms every consumer has vendored, the census deletes Claudinite's release plumbing automatically as part of migration retirement — no follow-up PR.
- **Secrets: nothing to migrate.** The four `CHROME_*` secrets already live in each consumer repo (they travel via `secrets: inherit` from the consumer's own workflow); Claudinite holds none.

## Plan

1. **Pack = source of truth.** Move the 4 workflows + 3 composite actions into `packs/chrome-extension-release/` as vendored templates; rewrite cross-repo `uses: missingbulb/Claudinite/.github/…@main` → local `uses: ./.github/…`; rename to avoid the in-repo filename collision (the orchestrator and the create-package reusable are both `chrome-extension-release.yml` today).
2. **Migration is the fix vehicle.** A new baseline migration carries: (a) a **materialize** op — baselining writes the vendored set into each consumer's `.github/` and drops the old thin-stub `@main` refs; (b) a **legacyPresent** probe ("still references `missingbulb/Claudinite/.github/workflows/chrome-extension-*`") for fleet telemetry; (c) a **retire-deletes-from-home** list — Claudinite's own release files. Extend the migration mechanism (today rename-only) with the materialize op, and teach the census to delete the home-repo files on retirement.
3. **Tolerant checks during transition.** The `cer/*` checks accept both the old thin-stub shape and the new vendored shape until the migration retires, so no consumer's check suite goes red mid-flight.
4. **Docs.** Update `RELEASE.md`, `.github/workflows/README.md` (drop the frozen-`@main`-API section), and the pack fingerprint.

## Prerequisite for the automatic cut

The automatic phase-2 deletion needs `FLEET_GITHUB_TOKEN` granted **Contents-write on the home repo** — #239 notes this is not granted yet. Until it is, the census logs "grant FLEET_GITHUB_TOKEN Contents write" and Claudinite's copies stay in place (harmless — consumers already run off their vendored copies by then).

Refs #270 (RELEASE item), #239 (token scope).","state":"open","html_url":"https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/issues/276","user":{"login":"missingbulb","id":73882448,"profile_url":"https://github.com/missingbulb","avatar_url":"https://avatars.githubusercontent.com/u/73882448?v=4"},"author_association":"OWNER","labels":["blocked"],"assignees":[],"comments":5,"reactions":{"total_count":0,"+1":0,"-1":0,"laugh":0,"confused":0,"heart":0,"hooray":0,"rocket":0,"eyes":0},"created_at":"2026-07-13T14:28:14Z","updated_at":"2026-08-22T05:13:24Z","has_parent":false,"has_children":false,"closed_by_pull_requests":{"total_count":0,"references":[]}}

{"number":170,"title":"Revisit: Workflow tool's interactive opt-in blocks unattended routines (waiting on Anthropic)","body":"## The limitation

The multi-agent-orchestration **`Workflow`** tool requires an **interactive human opt-in on every run** ("Allow Claude to run a workflow?"). That prompt only disappears under bypass-permissions / headless modes a scheduler can't be relied on to be in. Because an unattended routine has no human to click **Allow**, any routine that fans out through the Workflow tool stalls on step one.

This also means the tool's nicest ergonomics are off-limits to us for unattended work: committing a Workflow script and having the nightly job just run it by name (`Workflow({name: ...})`) hits the **same** prompt — the gate is on *invoking* a workflow, not on authoring one. And the parallel-agent step can't be pushed into a plain committed script either, since spawning Claude subagents is a harness capability, not something arbitrary code can call.

## Our current workaround

We fan the fleet daily maintenance routine out with **plain subagent dispatch** (the Agent/Task tool) instead, which carries no opt-in gate, and the orchestrator honors the phase barriers itself. See #168 / #169 and `routines/auto-all-repos-maintenance.md` + `skills/unattended-agents/SKILL.md`.

This works and is the right default (no dependency on an out-of-repo permission-mode setting), but it costs us the Workflow tool's built-in phase/barrier machinery and the option to run committed, reviewed orchestration code.

## Why keep this open

This is a limitation of the platform, not our code — we're **waiting on the world to change**. If Anthropic later lets an unattended session pre-authorize the Workflow tool (a settings allowlist entry, an environment/routine permission mode that reliably suppresses just this prompt, or persisted per-workflow consent that survives a fresh cloud clone), we could reconsider using committed Workflow scripts for the fleet routine and get determinism + review back.

**Action:** periodically check with Anthropic / the Claude Code release notes whether the Workflow tool can be pre-authorized for unattended sessions. When it can, revisit the plain-dispatch decision in the routine spec.

{"number":1149,"title":"converge-item.mjs cannot run from an MCP-only agent session","body":"`engine/scheduler/queue/instructions.md` step 6 tells the session executing a work item to run:

```
node /scheduler/queue/converge-item.mjs --issue  --outcome ... --summary ...
```

directly as a subprocess. That script (via `engine/scheduler/signals/gh.mjs`'s `makeGh`) talks to `api.github.com` straight over `fetch`, authorized with `process.env.GITHUB_TOKEN` — the Action-side credential, per the DESIGN comment atop `gh.mjs`: "engine/scheduler/ is the one place that legitimately uses the Action's GITHUB_TOKEN — everything session-side stays MCP-only."

But `queue/instructions.md` step 6 *is* session-side — it is the procedure every agent session follows to converge the one work item it was fired for (a Claude Code session, not an Actions job). This session's own system prompt states plainly it has no `gh` CLI and no direct GitHub API access, and must use the GitHub MCP server tools for all GitHub interactions. Confirmed live on this run (#1097):

- `GITHUB_REPOSITORY` is unset by default in this session (`converge-item: GITHUB_REPOSITORY is not set`).
- Setting it and calling the script directly returns a 403 straight from the GitHub REST API: `{"message":"GitHub access is not enabled for this session. An org admin must connect the Claude GitHub App for this organization."}` — a policy boundary, not a fixable env-var wrinkle.

This is the same class of break as #1133: a script written for the Actions-job execution context (`gh.mjs`'s `makeGh`) silently fails once the same work runs inside an MCP-only agent session — except here the break isn't silent, it's a hard stop on the one step every work item's session-side execution must perform: convergence. As written, no work item picked up by an agent session (`queue/instructions.md`'s normal path) can converge in code — it either gets hand-converged (which `instructions.md` explicitly says not to do) or sits stuck wearing `task:agent` until the janitor's 3h agent-leash reclaims it as dead.

1	// REMOVING A DIRECTORY GIT MAY STILL BE WRITING INTO.
2	//
3	// A recursive delete walks the tree and unlinks as it goes, so anything that
4	// appears in a directory between the walk and its rmdir makes the rmdir throw
5	// ENOTEMPTY. Git is a prolific source of exactly that: a `git` child that has
6	// returned still leaves its own housekeeping — auto-gc, packing, index and lock
7	// files under `.git/` — running for a moment afterwards, and under a parallel
8	// `node --test` there is always another core to run it on.
9	//
10	// The symptom is a delete that fails on a healthy tree, which reads as a broken
11	// test rather than a race: a red CI on a change that touched none of it. This
12	// repo has now closed that finding three times — #235, #258, and #1219 — each
13	// time by fixing the one call site that happened to fail, because each site
14	// spelled its own delete. So the retry lives HERE, once, and the sites that
15	// delete a git tree call this rather than rmSync.
16	//
17	// `maxRetries` is Node's own answer: rmSync retries EBUSY, EMFILE, ENFILE,
18	// ENOTEMPTY and EPERM with a linear backoff of `retryDelay` ms more each time.
19	// Three tries over ~300ms outlasts git's housekeeping without making a genuinely
20	// undeletable tree hang a run.
21	//
22	// It is the SECOND line of defense, not the first. Where the caller controls the
23	// git environment, keeping git's own background work in the foreground is the
24	// real fix — `GIT_ENV` in engine-tests/helpers.mjs does exactly that, and says so.
25	// This covers everything deleted by code that does not, or cannot, set it.

Base directory for this skill: /home/user/Claudinite/.claude/skills/extract-from-conversations

# Extract lessons from a conversation

The **dialogue** half of lesson extraction: read one agent ↔ user session — its turns *and* the actions
taken in it — and convert its friction into changes that make the **next** run faster, clearer, and less
dependent on human steering. Its sibling [extract-from-activity](../extract-from-activity/SKILL.md) mines
what the work committed; this one mines how the work went.

The **bar** a lesson must clear, the **local promotion ladder** it descends, and where a repo's capture
surface lives stay canonical in [extracting-lessons.md](../../extracting-lessons.md) — read it, don't
re-derive it. What follows is only what reading a *conversation* adds.

## The goal

Every pass optimizes for one outcome: **the next run needs less.** Less clarification, less rework, less
waiting, less human steering. Read the session not as "what did we accomplish" but as "where did this
cost more than it should have, and what durable change removes that cost next time." If a pass can't name
a concrete next-time saving, it found nothing — and that's fine.

## Where the conversation comes from

- **A captured log** on the repo's orphan `conversation-logs` branch (`<stamp>--issue-<n>--<session>.jsonl`),
  read with plain git in the checkout — `git show origin/conversation-logs:<file>`. The log carries
  per-entry timestamps, per-message token usage, and the `tool_use`/`tool_result` pairs behind every
  wall-time number, which is exactly what the measured analysis below needs. This is the routine path.
- **The live session**, when an owner asks in plain words for a retrospective. Same method; deliver the
  capture as a branch + PR **for a human to review**, never one that self-merges.

**Never reflect-and-edit unprompted in the middle of a task** — it interrupts the work; the owner decides
when a session is done enough to mine.

## What to look for — the friction signals

Read the conversation end to end and hunt for these signatures. Each marks a place the loop cost more than
necessary, and each converts to a specific durable fix.

### 1. Misunderstandings between agent and user

The signs: a clarifying-question round-trip; the user correcting an assumption ("no, I meant…"); the agent
building the wrong thing and reworking it; the user restating the same request; an `AskUserQuestion` whose
answer was, in hindsight, the obvious default.

**Convert to:** encode the resolved understanding so the next agent never has to ask. Every question the
user answered is a candidate **default**; every correction is a candidate **convention or glossary entry**;
a recurring wrong assumption is a candidate **confirm-first checkpoint placed earlier**, or a clearer doc
the agent reads cold and gets right the first time. The test of a good fix: next time the agent proceeds
correctly **without the round-trip**.

### 2. Suboptimal agent actions

The signs: the agent took an approach then backtracked; did redundant or repeated work; re-ran a command
that had already failed for a knowable reason; reached for a heavy tool where a light one fit; reinvented
something the codebase already provided; re-read a file it had just written to "verify"; missed an existing
convention and had it corrected in review.

**Convert to:** a rule pointing at the right approach or tool, a pointer to the existing helper/convention
so it's found first, or a **footgun note placed where it'll be read** (the usage-site-vs-central call is in
[extracting-lessons.md](../../extracting-lessons.md)). The test: next time the agent takes the good path
first, not after a detour.

### 3. Long wall-time waits — and measure them

The signs: independent operations run **serially** that had no dependency and could have been parallel; a
padded fixed `sleep` that over- or under-shot; a process **waited out after its result was already in
hand**; blind long polling; re-running a check (e.g. CI) that was already green.

**Measure, don't hand-wave.** Quantify the wait with real wall-clock numbers from the log's own timestamps
and separate the kinds of time — compute (a compile, a test/render run) vs. genuine **idle waiting**
(sleeps, polling, a finished process not yet killed). The numbers are computable, never estimated. A fix is
only credible against numbers; name the **single highest-leverage change** that shortens it, or conclude it
was already optimal.

**Convert to:** a batch/parallelize rule, a poll-with-rolling-backoff instead of a blind sleep,
kill-the-process-once-its-output-is-in-hand, or merge-on-an-already-green-check. (These are the subject of
the standing **efficiency analysis** in [the unattended-agents skill](../unattended-agents/SKILL.md) — fold
a wall-time finding into that frame rather than re-deriving it.) The test: same result, less wall clock, no
loss of quality.

## Encode the questions the user keeps asking

The single highest-leverage move for **less human feedback**: the questions a user asks *repeatedly* are a
checklist the agent should run **itself.** If the user keeps asking "how many processes ran — could it be
fewer?", "what took longest?", "did you kill it the moment its work was done?", stop waiting to be asked —
fold those exact questions into a **standing self-check the agent answers proactively** at the end of the
relevant work, and close with a terse verdict (a concrete change, or an explicit "already optimal"). Each
recurring question converted this way is one the user never has to ask again — and it's where a *measured*
retrospective comes from: the user's recurring efficiency questions, answered pre-emptively, with numbers.

## Two windows per run: the newest day, and the oldest day still on the branch

Every run reads exactly two sets of captures, both taken from the filename stamps:

- **the last 24 hours** — the fresh pass, over what was captured since the previous run;
- **the first 24 hours on the branch** — every capture stamped within 24h of the oldest one still there.
  This is the hindsight pass, and it is a real re-read rather than a formality: a friction signal that
  looked situational when it was fresh may have recurred since, and a lesson landed since may have made a
  keeper redundant. Both directions are legitimate outcomes, and corpus dedup makes the overlap harmless.

The two windows are also what keeps deletion honest. Retention is an agentless task that prunes on the
stamp alone, with no handshake back to this one — safe because the branch is read from its oldest end
every run, so a capture reaches retention having been read. Reading less than the oldest window silently
breaks that; reading more is only wasted effort.

## Provenance: summarize the exchange, never paste it

For each rule that actually **lands** from a log, post one short comment on the issue the log names
(`--issue-<n>--` in its filename; **`--issue-0--` means the capture had no associated issue**, so there is
nothing to post on and the rule simply lands without a comment):

- one provenance line — the rule added, the capture date, the session id;
- then a **200-word-max** description of just the slice of conversation that caused the rule: what was
  asked, what went wrong or got corrected, and why the rule follows from it.

**Summarize, never transcribe.** The dialogue itself is far too verbose for an issue — no pasted turns
beyond a short quoted phrase, never raw JSONL, never a rendered transcript. A log that yields nothing gets
**no** comment: extraction is the only path to permanence, and a log's conversation is gone once retention
deletes it. That is a deliberate call, so a padded "lesson" written to feel productive costs more than the
silence it replaced.

Base directory for this skill: /home/user/Claudinite/.claude/skills/extract-from-conversations

# Extract lessons from a conversation

The **dialogue** half of lesson extraction: read one agent ↔ user session — its turns *and* the actions
taken in it — and convert its friction into changes that make the **next** run faster, clearer, and less
dependent on human steering. Its sibling [extract-from-activity](../extract-from-activity/SKILL.md) mines
what the work committed; this one mines how the work went.

The **bar** a lesson must clear, the **local promotion ladder** it descends, and where a repo's capture
surface lives stay canonical in [extracting-lessons.md](../../extracting-lessons.md) — read it, don't
re-derive it. What follows is only what reading a *conversation* adds.

## The goal

Every pass optimizes for one outcome: **the next run needs less.** Less clarification, less rework, less
waiting, less human steering. Read the session not as "what did we accomplish" but as "where did this
cost more than it should have, and what durable change removes that cost next time." If a pass can't name
a concrete next-time saving, it found nothing — and that's fine.

## Where the conversation comes from

- **A captured log** on the repo's orphan `conversation-logs` branch (`<stamp>--issue-<n>--<session>.jsonl`),
  read with plain git in the checkout — `git show origin/conversation-logs:<file>`. The log carries
  per-entry timestamps, per-message token usage, and the `tool_use`/`tool_result` pairs behind every
  wall-time number, which is exactly what the measured analysis below needs. This is the routine path.
- **The live session**, when an owner asks in plain words for a retrospective. Same method; deliver the
  capture as a branch + PR **for a human to review**, never one that self-merges.

**Never reflect-and-edit unprompted in the middle of a task** — it interrupts the work; the owner decides
when a session is done enough to mine.

## What to look for — the friction signals

Read the conversation end to end and hunt for these signatures. Each marks a place the loop cost more than
necessary, and each converts to a specific durable fix.

### 1. Misunderstandings between agent and user

The signs: a clarifying-question round-trip; the user correcting an assumption ("no, I meant…"); the agent
building the wrong thing and reworking it; the user restating the same request; an `AskUserQuestion` whose
answer was, in hindsight, the obvious default.

**Convert to:** encode the resolved understanding so the next agent never has to ask. Every question the
user answered is a candidate **default**; every correction is a candidate **convention or glossary entry**;
a recurring wrong assumption is a candidate **confirm-first checkpoint placed earlier**, or a clearer doc
the agent reads cold and gets right the first time. The test of a good fix: next time the agent proceeds
correctly **without the round-trip**.

### 2. Suboptimal agent actions

The signs: the agent took an approach then backtracked; did redundant or repeated work; re-ran a command
that had already failed for a knowable reason; reached for a heavy tool where a light one fit; reinvented
something the codebase already provided; re-read a file it had just written to "verify"; missed an existing
convention and had it corrected in review.

**Convert to:** a rule pointing at the right approach or tool, a pointer to the existing helper/convention
so it's found first, or a **footgun note placed where it'll be read** (the usage-site-vs-central call is in
[extracting-lessons.md](../../extracting-lessons.md)). The test: next time the agent takes the good path
first, not after a detour.

### 3. Long wall-time waits — and measure them

The signs: independent operations run **serially** that had no dependency and could have been parallel; a
padded fixed `sleep` that over- or under-shot; a process **waited out after its result was already in
hand**; blind long polling; re-running a check (e.g. CI) that was already green.

**Measure, don't hand-wave.** Quantify the wait with real wall-clock numbers from the log's own timestamps
and separate the kinds of time — compute (a compile, a test/render run) vs. genuine **idle waiting**
(sleeps, polling, a finished process not yet killed). The numbers are computable, never estimated. A fix is
only credible against numbers; name the **single highest-leverage change** that shortens it, or conclude it
was already optimal.

**Convert to:** a batch/parallelize rule, a poll-with-rolling-backoff instead of a blind sleep,
kill-the-process-once-its-output-is-in-hand, or merge-on-an-already-green-check. (These are the subject of
the standing **efficiency analysis** in [the unattended-agents skill](../unattended-agents/SKILL.md) — fold
a wall-time finding into that frame rather than re-deriving it.) The test: same result, less wall clock, no
loss of quality.

## Encode the questions the user keeps asking

The single highest-leverage move for **less human feedback**: the questions a user asks *repeatedly* are a
checklist the agent should run **itself.** If the user keeps asking "how many processes ran — could it be
fewer?", "what took longest?", "did you kill it the moment its work was done?", stop waiting to be asked —
fold those exact questions into a **standing self-check the agent answers proactively** at the end of the
relevant work, and close with a terse verdict (a concrete change, or an explicit "already optimal"). Each
recurring question converted this way is one the user never has to ask again — and it's where a *measured*
retrospective comes from: the user's recurring efficiency questions, answered pre-emptively, with numbers.

## Two windows per run: the newest day, and the oldest day still on the branch

Every run reads exactly two sets of captures, both taken from the filename stamps:

- **the last 24 hours** — the fresh pass, over what was captured since the previous run;
- **the first 24 hours on the branch** — every capture stamped within 24h of the oldest one still there.
  This is the hindsight pass, and it is a real re-read rather than a formality: a friction signal that
  looked situational when it was fresh may have recurred since, and a lesson landed since may have made a
  keeper redundant. Both directions are legitimate outcomes, and corpus dedup makes the overlap harmless.

The two windows are also what keeps deletion honest. Retention is an agentless task that prunes on the
stamp alone, with no handshake back to this one — safe because the branch is read from its oldest end
every run, so a capture reaches retention having been read. Reading less than the oldest window silently
breaks that; reading more is only wasted effort.

## Provenance: summarize the exchange, never paste it

For each rule that actually **lands** from a log, post one short comment on the issue the log names
(`--issue-<n>--` in its filename; **`--issue-0--` means the capture had no associated issue**, so there is
nothing to post on and the rule simply lands without a comment):

- one provenance line — the rule added, the capture date, the session id;
- then a **200-word-max** description of just the slice of conversation that caused the rule: what was
  asked, what went wrong or got corrected, and why the rule follows from it.

**Summarize, never transcribe.** The dialogue itself is far too verbose for an issue — no pasted turns
beyond a short quoted phrase, never raw JSONL, never a rendered transcript. A log that yields nothing gets
**no** comment: extraction is the only path to permanence, and a log's conversation is gone once retention
deletes it. That is a deliberate call, so a padded "lesson" written to feel productive costs more than the
silence it replaced.

7	## Standing owner decisions — settled, do not re-litigate
8	
9	- **Wanting a rule about what the `packs/` tree may reference** — declare and configure the
10	  `barriers` pack, extending it generically if a capability is missing. Never write standalone
11	  code that checks packs-tree segregation.
12	
13	- **Writing a `docs/<initiative>/DESIGN.md`** — the end state and its rationale only, with
14	  alternatives and their drawbacks; never requests, prior-state narrative, or owner opinions.
15	  The migration is work, not a document: its phased plan, status and remaining work live in the
16	  tracking issue (`writing-migration-plans`), never in a sibling `MIGRATION.md`.
17	
18	- **A `docs/<initiative>/DESIGN.md` whose system is now built** — its content duplicates the
19	  module headers and pack `README.md`s that must independently state the same facts once the
20	  pipeline exists, so a design doc that survives the build only has to be kept in sync with both.
21	  Verify each section actually lives there before touching anything; move what has no other
22	  home (an owner-decision record with its rationale is typically the one irreplaceable part),
23	  sweep every `§`-numbered pointer into a pack-README reference (or drop it where the sentence
24	  only cited itself), and delete the doc whole rather than trim it. Don't extend the sweep to a
25	  design doc that still describes work in flight, or a much larger one many module headers cite
26	  by section — decide those separately rather than discover the scale mid-run (#1169).
27	
28	- **Ending a session on unfinished work** — write the state into the tracking issue. The
29	  owner's opener is `continue work on #<n>`, so anything else is lost; never compose a hand-off
30	  prompt.
31	
32	- **Designing anything that spans repos** — split it: a self-contained per-repo half in the
33	  canon, the aggregation half as a Shepherd fleet task. No repo list exists anywhere in canon
34	  code; Shepherd enumerates members at runtime. A derived fleet artifact lands there as a daily
35	  auto-merged PR of a `GENERATED` file, never a commit to its `main`.
36	
37	- **Choosing a value right for nearly every project** — keep it in the pack's own code: ask
38	  nothing at adoption, write nothing into the member's config. Read config as optional — an
39	  unset key means the default, never "misconfigured".
40	
41	- **Needing a member to flip a platform setting or hold a wider credential** — last resort:
42	  per-repo manual work reliably does not happen, and the capability then dies silently in every
43	  repo nobody configured. Prefer the route that works with the Action's own `GITHUB_TOKEN`, and
44	  neutralise a blocking platform behaviour's *effect* rather than asking for the platform to be
45	  reconfigured. Where nothing weaker can work (`FLEET_GITHUB_TOKEN`), name the exact scope and
46	  have the automation report when it is missing rather than degrade silently.
47	
48	- **Landing a change to what members receive** — force delivery in the same session only when
49	  *"will it work on every repo?"* is a live question: the answer turns on how members differ —
50	  engine flow, a contract their own files must satisfy, a stub or workflow, a migration record, a
51	  new config key. Then drive Shepherd's `fleet-baseline` with `follow`, report per member unasked,
52	  and attach the repos that verification needs rather than offering to; a dispatch is not a result,
53	  and 204 means queued. Where the change is uniform by construction — prose, a doc, a move of
54	  something nothing executes from the mount — the nightly converge *is* the delivery, and forcing
55	  buys noise rather than assurance.
56	
57	- **Retiring a field, option or module** — `@deprecated` on its definition, plus a comment at
58	  each sanctioned holdout's declaration site saying why it still carries the field. Never a
59	  bespoke conformance check for a deprecation. Keep the contract validating the lingering field.
60	
61	- **Wanting a `.claudinite-settings.json` entry's config validated** — that is a real JSON Schema
62	  the file points at with `$schema`, checked by ordinary tooling. Never a coded per-pack
63	  validation vocabulary or a bespoke `configSchema` type system on the manifest — built and
64	  reverted in #919 ("That's why we have schemas").
65	
66	- **Wanting to share logic between two sibling packs** — never put it in `engine/`, which breaks
67	  the package-manager model, and never make one pack depend on the other, which is what breaks
68	  pack independence. First check whether the sharing is even necessary — self-describing data
69	  (each side states its own field vocabulary) can remove the need to interpret another pack's
70	  format at all. Where identical code is still needed, consider duplicating it, possibly with a
71	  drift guard; sometimes duplication between packs is fine (#959: "why do you even need a drift
72	  guard? Just write the json. Don't overkill.").
73	
74	- **Surfacing a number a human reads as a report card** (a dashboard tile, a digest, a fleet
75	  rollup) — never a monotonic cumulative total, which says nothing about today, and never a figure
76	  nothing measures (no estimated hours saved, no score). Report a **window against the previous
77	  window**. Where a field can't be had from the reads already being made, name it as absent in the
78	  surface's own note rather than approximating it: a stated gap is information, a guess is not
79	  (owner, #1001). Before windowing a count, check whether it is built from an event log or from a
80	  point-in-time **stamp**: windowing a stamp-derived figure (e.g. "members that converged last
81	  week", counted from each member's single last-converge date) can read a steady, healthy
82	  population as declining purely from where stamps land relative to the window boundary — reserve
83	  the window-over-window shape for counts genuinely built from things that happened inside the
84	  window (#1008).
85	
86	- **Classifying an issue or work item by deriving it structurally from other live state** (a
87	  title match against what's declared at HEAD, a computed membership test) — reconsider once the
88	  derivation's own inputs can mutate while the classified object stays open. A "standing vs
89	  ad-hoc" task classification computed live from whether an issue's title matched a task declared
90	  at HEAD silently reinterpreted an open issue's own history the moment that task's frequency or
91	  name changed underneath it. An explicit marker stamped once at creation and never revisited
92	  doesn't have that failure mode — the general preference for a structural classifier over a
93	  hand-set field holds only for state that isn't itself still in flight (#1120).
94	
95	- **Scheduling the removal of a temporary compatibility tolerance** (an old-format reader, a
96	  legacy-field fallback) — gate the removal on a converge-cycle-confirmable precondition ("no
97	  member still stamps the legacy format"), never a calendar date alone. Retiring the tolerance
98	  while a member is still on the old format doesn't just leave that member behind: the value it
99	  stamps starts reading as "no version installed" to the now-stricter reader, which re-applies
100	  every migration record in the corpus (#1106).

102	## Working with the owner and the session's tools
103	
104	- **Answering "why did it fail?"** — lead with the throwing call site: `file:line`, the
105	  function, and which side enforced it. A correct narrative that never names the line reads as
106	  unanswered.
107	
108	- **Reaching for `AskUserQuestion`** — it blocks for minutes (~170s median), so spend it only
109	  on a fork you cannot take back. Anything answerable from the instruction, the tree, or a
110	  reversible default: answer it, act, and say what you assumed. Never re-post a question that was
111	  declined — take its recommended default, or open the question up.
112	
113	- **Being asked to generalise something, or to review it** — land the conversions or action
114	  points it unlocks in the same change. A capability ships with the caller that exercises it; an
115	  analysis ships with the first of its recommendations applied.
116	
117	- **Calling anything on `Claude_Code_Remote`** — one call per intent, ever. Each costs
118	  minutes, and a call that returns nothing has *not* failed — the retry has run to 81% of a
119	  session's tool wall-clock. For "is it green yet" read the check status directly; to read a
120	  public sibling repo, `git clone --depth 1` (~2s), since `add_repo` attaches nothing the git
121	  proxy doesn't already serve.
122	
123	- **Waiting for something to happen** — the guard must name the condition awaited (a run's
124	  status, a file's arrival, a deadline), with no trailing padded `sleep`. A guard you wouldn't
125	  write as the *whole* test means you are sleeping and calling it polling. **Exception: GitHub
126	  CI/PR check status is not this repo's case for `Monitor` or a `curl`/shell poll loop** — this
127	  sandbox proxy-blocks `api.github.com`, so both silently report "still running" until they time
128	  out (measured ~26 minutes lost across two PRs waiting past an already-green check, #880). Read
129	  the head sha's check runs with the GitHub MCP tool instead. Poll it on a rolling backoff, or
130	  not at all when a background watcher already reports that signal.
131	
132	- **Writing a step a human must do by hand into an issue** — when asking for a manual action,
133	  make absolutely sure it is needed: a checklist whose items are mostly no-ops teaches the reader
134	  to skim it, exactly what the checklist exists to prevent. Make the breadcrumb trail a
135	  hyperlink, to the deepest existing settings URL — a link keeps working or redirects where a
136	  written-out trail goes stale the moment GitHub reorganizes the page (#952, owner-authored).
137	
138	- **Replying to an owner comment that raises more than one claim** — answer **every** claim in
139	  that first reply, including the one you intend to push back on. A claim left silently
140	  unaddressed, even when the rest of the reply is right, just makes the owner re-raise it later
141	  (#864: a placement objection went unanswered for 55 minutes before the owner repeated it).
142	
143	- **Repeating a design doc's stated architectural rationale** — verify each of its claimed
144	  grounds against the current code (declared secrets, executor permissions) before reciting it
145	  again, especially once a direct challenge has already found it wrong once. The same overstated
146	  "a task structurally cannot hold this permission" argument was corrected twice in one session —
147	  once for a GitHub Pages deploy, again minutes later for a chrome-extension release — because
148	  code-work already runs inside the executor's own Action job with the permissions in question
149	  (#1069).
150	
151	- **An owner reversing a standing decision** — the fix is not answering the question that
152	  prompted it, it is finding and purging every place in the repo (docs, comments, code defaults)
153	  that still states the old decision, and recording the new one where a future session reads it
154	  before ever asserting the stale version again. One reversal (turning local scheduling on,
155	  moving `canon-curation`) had to be repeated five times before a session treated it as a
156	  durable-artifact problem rather than a one-off answer (#364).
157	
158	- **Firing `AskUserQuestion` on a vague, destructive-sounding instruction** ("remove the entire
159	  mechanism," "get rid of the whole thing") — scope the question to pin down the boundary of the
160	  vague noun itself, not just the downstream consequences of one reading of it. A question that
161	  asked only what happens to the one dependent check, while silently assuming "entire mechanism"
162	  meant the whole engine surface, let 15 minutes of deletion, test-authoring and PR/issue
163	  bookkeeping land before the owner caught it nine minutes later and all of it was discarded with
164	  a hard reset (#1114).
